column1: Why are fully connected neural networks parameter-inefficient for large images?
column2: They connect every pixel to every hidden unit, ignoring that spatial correlation in images is local.

column1: How many parameters are required for a fully connected layer with $1\text{M}$ hidden units given a $1000 \times 1000$ image?
column2: It requires $10^{12}$ parameters.

column1: In image processing, what is meant by 'stationarity'?
column2: The assumption that image statistics and features are similar across different spatial locations.

column1: What structural modification defines a locally connected neural network compared to a fully connected network?
column2: Units only connect to a small local patch (receptive field) of the input image.

column1: How many parameters does a locally connected layer with $1\text{M}$ hidden units and a $10 \times 10$ filter size have?
column2: It has $100\text{M}$ parameters ($10^6 \times 100$).

column1: What additional constraint does a convolutional layer apply to a locally connected layer?
column2: Parameter sharing across all spatial locations using learned kernels.

column1: How many parameters are needed for a convolutional layer with $100$ filters of size $10 \times 10$ (ignoring bias)?
column2: It requires $10\text{K}$ parameters ($100 \times 100$).

column1: What spatial operation defines 2D discrete image convolution?
column2: Replacing each pixel with a linear combination of its spatial neighbours weighted by a filter kernel.

column1: Which two fundamental properties define a linear system $T$?
column2: Homogeneity ($T[aX] = aT[X]$) and Additivity ($T[X_1 + X_2] = T[X_1] + T[X_2]$).

column1: What mathematical principle unifies homogeneity and additivity in linear systems?
column2: The principle of superposition ($T[aX_1 + bX_2] = aT[X_1] + bT[X_2]$).

column1: What is the formula to calculate the spatial output dimension $W_{\text{out}}$ of a convolutional layer?
column2: $W_{\text{out}} = \frac{W - K + 2P}{S} + 1$, where $W$ is input size, $K$ is filter size, $P$ is padding, and $S$ is stride.

column1: Given an input volume of $32 \times 32 \times 3$, what is the output spatial size after applying $10$ filters of size $5 \times 5$ with stride $1$ and padding $2$?
column2: The spatial output size is $32 \times 32$.

column1: Given an input volume of $32 \times 32 \times 3$, what is the full output volume shape after applying $10$ filters of size $5 \times 5$ with stride $1$ and padding $2$?
column2: The output volume shape is $32 \times 32 \times 10$.

column1: How many trainable parameters (including bias) are in a single filter of size $5 \times 5 \times 3$?
column2: It contains $76$ parameters ($5 \times 5 \times 3 + 1$).

column1: How many total trainable parameters are in a convolutional layer with $10$ filters of size $5 \times 5 \times 3$ (including bias)?
column2: It contains $760$ parameters ($76 \times 10$).

column1: What determines the channel depth of an activation map volume resulting from a convolution layer?
column2: The number of distinct convolutional filters applied to the input.

column1: In human neuroanatomy, what is 'retinotopy'?
column2: The topographical mapping where adjacent cells in the visual cortex represent adjacent regions in the visual field.

column1: Which visual brain area processes basic visual features such as vertical, horizontal, and angular edges?
column2: The primary visual cortex (V1).

column1: What simple 1D derivative filter can be used to detect a step edge in a 1D signal?
column2: A filter with weights $[-1, 1]$ (or $[-1, 0, 1]$).

column1: What is the output of a 1D edge detection filter when applied across a region of constant signal values?
column2: The output is zero.

column1: Early neural network architecture: Cognitron/Neocognitron
column2: Definition: Early bio-inspired network models for pattern recognition introduced by Fukushima (1971–1982).

column1: Who introduced hierarchical pooling mechanisms inspired by the visual cortex in 1999?
column2: Riesenhuber and Poggio.

column1: Which seminal paper introduced LeNet-5 for document recognition?
column2: LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, and Haffner (1998).

column1: What are the four core feed-forward operations in a traditional LeNet-style architecture?
column2: Convolution, non-linearity (rectification), pooling (subsampling), and fully connected layers.

column1: How are convolutional filters trained in supervised CNNs like LeNet?
column2: By back-propagating classification errors to update filter weights.

column1: What is the primary function of a pooling layer in a Convolutional Neural Network?
column2: To downsample spatial dimensions, making representations smaller, more manageable, and spatially invariant.

column1: How does a pooling layer process multi-channel feature map volumes?
column2: It operates independently over each depth slice/channel of the activation map.

column1: What is the output of a $2 \times 2$ Max Pooling filter applied to the matrix block $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$?
column2: The output value is $6$.

column1: Applying a $2 \times 2$ max pooling filter with stride $2$ reduces a $224 \times 224 \times 64$ activation map to what dimensions?
column2: It reduces the volume to $112 \times 112 \times 64$.

column1: Who authored the 2012 AlexNet paper that sparked the deep learning revolution in computer vision?
column2: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton.

column1: Approximately how many parameters and neurons did AlexNet (2012) contain?
column2: It contained approximately $60$ million parameters and $650,000$ neurons.

column1: What regularization technique was key in preventing overfitting in AlexNet?
column2: Dropout.

column1: Which hardware advancement enabled a $50\times$ training speedup for AlexNet compared to CPU implementations?
column2: Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).

column1: How did the training dataset scale increase from LeNet (1998) to AlexNet (2012)?
column2: It increased from $10^3$ images (MNIST) to $10^6$ images (ImageNet).

column1: What trend in filter size and network depth emerged in architectures following AlexNet (e.g., VGG, ResNet)?
column2: A shift towards using smaller filters ($3 \times 3$) and building deeper architectures.

column1: Why are smaller filters preferred over larger filters in deep CNN architectures?
column2: They are easier to learn, introduce more non-linearities, and use fewer parameters for the same receptive field.

column1: How many layers are in the VGG architecture shown in the 2014 ImageNet challenge progression?
column2: 19 layers.

column1: How many layers are in the GoogLeNet architecture from 2014?
column2: 22 layers.

column1: How many layers are in the ResNet architecture introduced in 2015?
column2: 152 layers.

column1: What is meant by the 'receptive field' of an output unit in a CNN?
column2: The spatial region in the input volume that directly influences the activation of that unit.

column1: How much does a single convolutional layer with kernel size $K$ add to the receptive field size?
column2: It adds $K - 1$ to the receptive field size.

column1: What is the formula for the receptive field size of a network with $L$ convolutional layers, each having kernel size $K$?
column2: The receptive field size is $1 + L \times (K - 1)$.

column1: What is the receptive field size in the input after $3$ stacked convolutional layers with $3 \times 3$ kernels?
column2: The receptive field size is $7 \times 7$ ($1 + 3 \times (3 - 1)$).

column1: What technique provides visual explanations for CNN predictions via gradient-based localization (Selvaraju et al.)?
column2: Grad-CAM.

column1: What visual explanation methodology was proposed by Chattopadhyay et al. (2018) as an enhancement to Grad-CAM?
column2: Grad-CAM++.

column1: What black-box visual explanation technique uses randomized input sampling (Petsiuk et al., 2018)?
column2: RISE (Randomized Input Sampling for Explanation).

column1: The property where applying a system transformation to scaled inputs equals scaling the transformed output is _____.
column2: Homogeneity

column1: The visual cortex area VO1 primarily handles visual processing near which eccentricity range shown in retinotopy maps?
column2: Peripheral and central visual field regions beyond early visual areas V1–V3.

column1: What happens to spatial dimensionality during subsampling/pooling in LeNet?
column2: The spatial height and width of feature maps are reduced, aggregating local features.

column1: Concept: Spatial locality in images
column2: Definition: The assumption that pixels close to each other are strongly correlated, whereas distant pixels are less related.

column1: Why is parameter sharing mathematically valid across an image?
column2: Because local feature statistics (e.g. edges, textures) are translation-invariant across spatial locations.

column1: What is the primary trade-off when using a stride $S > 1$ in a convolutional layer?
column2: It downsamples the spatial resolution of the feature map, reducing computational overhead.

column1: In a $32 \times 32 \times 3$ input image, what does the depth dimension '3' represent?
column2: The three color channels (Red, Green, Blue).

column1: How does doubling the number of filters in a convolutional layer affect the output feature map?
column2: It doubles the depth channel dimension of the output activation map volume.
